planting.note: Direct sow or transplant seedlings into a warm, flooded paddy bed well after soil has warmed; Kalijira is a long-season photoperiod-sensitive landrace traditionally harvested in the aman (monsoon) season in Bangladesh.

directions: Kalijira is a tall, fine-grained aromatic rice landrace long grown in the floodplain districts of Bangladesh, prized for its small, slender grains that are traditionally used whole (never parboiled and polished down like ordinary rice) in pulao and biryani because they hold their shape and release a distinct aroma when cooked in ghee and whole spices. The name translates roughly to 'black cumin,' a reference to the grain's small, dark, cumin-seed-like appearance before milling. Plants are tall and lodging-prone compared to modern dwarf varieties, so give them a sheltered flooded bed, standing water through most of the vegetative season, and full sun with steady warmth for a long tropical growing season. Because it is strongly photoperiod-sensitive, Kalijira flowers in response to shortening daylength in late summer and is best suited to regions with a Bangladesh-like monsoon-season growing calendar or greenhouse daylength control.
sources: Bangladesh Rice Research Institute (BRRI), aromatic and fine rice landrace documentation
International Rice Research Institute (IRRI) Genesys germplasm database
Bangladesh Agricultural Research Council, indigenous rice landrace surveys

planting.note: Direct sow or transplant into warm, flooded paddy beds well after soil has warmed; like other Bangladeshi fine-grain aromatics, Chinigura is photoperiod-sensitive and traditionally grown on a monsoon-season (aman) calendar.

directions: Chinigura is a small-grained aromatic rice landrace traditionally associated with the greater Dinajpur region of northern Bangladesh, where it has long been the preferred rice for special-occasion biryani and polao alongside Kalijira. Its name means roughly 'sugar-curl,' describing the tiny, curved, sugar-grain-like shape of the uncooked kernel, which swells only modestly on cooking and keeps a firm, separate texture that Bengali cooks value for layered rice dishes. The tall, slender plants are lodging-prone and lower-yielding than modern semidwarf rice, so they are usually grown in sheltered paddy beds with standing water maintained through tillering and heading. Give it a long, hot, humid growing season and full sun, and expect flowering to be triggered by shortening days in late summer in regions where daylength tracks the South Asian monsoon calendar.
sources: Bangladesh Rice Research Institute (BRRI), fine and aromatic rice germplasm catalogues
International Rice Research Institute (IRRI) Genesys germplasm database
Bangladesh Agricultural Research Institute, indigenous landrace characterization studies

common_name: Jumli Marsi Rice (Nepali High-Altitude Red Rice Landrace)

planting.note: Transplant seedlings into a cool, flooded bed once hard frost risk has passed; Jumli Marsi is remarkable among rice landraces for tolerating the cool nights and short summer of high mountain valleys, traditionally grown around 2,300-3,050 m elevation in Nepal's Jumla district.

directions: Jumli Marsi is a red-bran rice landrace grown by hill farmers in the Jumla district of far-western Nepal, famous for being cultivated at some of the highest elevations of any rice in the world, in cool mountain valleys where few other rice types can mature before frost. The grain has a reddish bran layer, a nutty flavor, and is traditionally cooked whole as a staple or milled for distinctive red rice dishes and local rice wine. Because it has adapted to short, cool growing seasons it tolerates lower water temperatures than lowland tropical rice, but it still needs a flooded or saturated paddy bed and full sun to fill its grain before autumn cold arrives. This landrace has been the subject of geographic-indication recognition efforts in Nepal and is maintained by regional seed banks as an example of cold-tolerant rice genetics.
sources: Nepal Agricultural Research Council (NARC), rice landrace and genetic resource documentation
LI-BIRD (Local Initiatives for Biodiversity, Research and Development), Nepal agrobiodiversity surveys
Bioversity International, in-situ conservation studies of Nepali rice landraces

planting.note: Plant a grafted tree in spring in full sun in deep, well-drained soil; Chaunsa is one of Pakistan's best-known commercial mango cultivars, centered on the Multan region of southern Punjab.

directions: Chaunsa is one of the most widely exported Pakistani mango cultivars, grown predominantly around Multan in southern Punjab and ripening late in the mango season, from roughly mid-July into August, after most other Pakistani cultivars have finished. The fruit is medium-to-large with a smooth, thin, golden-yellow skin and intensely sweet, fiberless, fine-textured flesh with relatively little fiber and a small, flat seed. Trees are vigorous and productive, and because the cultivar ripens in the hottest part of the Punjab summer it depends on strong heat accumulation to develop full sweetness. Give it full sun, deep well-drained soil, and complete protection from any frost, since it has no cold hardiness.
sources: Pakistan Agricultural Research Council, mango cultivar documentation
University of Florida IFAS Extension, mango cultivar references
Punjab Agriculture Department (Pakistan), Multan mango belt horticulture reports

common_name: Anwar Ratol Mango (Pakistani Punjab Dessert Mango)

planting.note: Plant a grafted tree in spring in full sun in deep, well-drained soil; Anwar Ratol is a small-fruited, early-season Pakistani Punjab dessert mango grown mainly around Rahim Yar Khan and other southern Punjab orchards.

directions: Anwar Ratol traces to the village of Ratol, which lay in pre-partition Punjab and is now on the Indian side of the border, but the cultivar has been propagated and commercially grown for decades in Pakistani Punjab, where it is regarded as one of the finest early-season dessert mangoes. Fruit is small to medium, thin-skinned, and very sweet with soft, fiberless flesh and an intense, perfume-like aroma, though the thin skin makes it bruise-prone and poorly suited to long shipping compared to tougher-skinned commercial types. Trees bear relatively early in the Pakistani mango season, ahead of Chaunsa and Sindhri. Give it full sun, deep well-drained soil, and complete frost protection, and handle ripe fruit gently since the thin peel splits and bruises easily.
sources: Pakistan Agricultural Research Council, mango cultivar documentation
University of Florida IFAS Extension, mango cultivar references
Punjab Agriculture Department (Pakistan), horticulture extension mango variety profiles

planting.note: Plant a grafted tree in spring in full sun in deep, well-drained soil; Sindhri is the signature mango cultivar of Sindh province, Pakistan, centered on the Mirpurkhas district, and ripens in the main mid-summer flush of the Pakistani mango season.

directions: Sindhri is often called the 'Queen of Mangoes' in Pakistan and is the flagship cultivar of the Mirpurkhas district of Sindh province, a region considered one of the country's premier mango-growing belts. The fruit is large and elongated with smooth, golden-yellow skin and sweet, fiberless, deep-orange flesh, and it ripens in the heart of the summer mango season when Sindh's intense heat concentrates sugars in the fruit. Trees are vigorous and productive under the hot, arid Sindh climate, and the cultivar is a major component of Pakistan's mango export trade to the Middle East, Europe, and beyond. Give it full sun, deep well-drained soil, consistent irrigation through fruit development, and complete protection from any frost.
sources: Pakistan Agricultural Research Council, mango cultivar documentation
Sindh Agriculture Department (Pakistan), Mirpurkhas mango belt horticulture reports
University of Florida IFAS Extension, mango cultivar references

planting.note: Plant a grafted tree in spring in full sun in deep, well-drained soil; Fazli is a late-ripening Bangladeshi mango cultivar centered on the Rajshahi and Chapainawabganj mango belt, bearing after most other regional cultivars have finished.

directions: Fazli is a large, late-season mango cultivar strongly associated with the Rajshahi and Chapainawabganj districts of northern Bangladesh, a mango belt whose fruit received geographical-indication recognition from the Bangladeshi government. The fruit is notably large, often exceeding a pound, with firm, fiberless, mildly sweet flesh that holds up well in transport and is valued for its late harvest window, extending the regional mango season into August when earlier cultivars are gone. Trees are vigorous and heavy-bearing, and the fruit's thick skin and firm flesh make it one of the more shelf-stable traditional South Asian mango cultivars. Give it full sun, deep well-drained soil, and complete frost protection, since it has no cold tolerance.
sources: Bangladesh Department of Agricultural Extension, Rajshahi mango belt variety documentation
Bangladesh geographical indication (GI) registration records for Rajshahi mangoes
University of Florida IFAS Extension, mango cultivar references
